notes: \cpara{Opens the memoir: the parents answered the child's arguments, including arguments against Judaism, by appeal to experience, and the child stopped arguing with them.}

\cfact{The research meant is presumably work such as Mueller and Dweck (1998), whose abstract reports that ``praise for intelligence had more negative consequences for students' achievement motivation than praise for effort.''}
\cpara{Gives the parents' general formula: experience, maturity and wisdom count for more than intelligence.}
\cpara{A joke: as reverse psychology, the formula worked, and taught the child to value intelligence above all.}
\cpara{Adds that it was not a plan, and that the result was not good.}

\cpara{Gives the older author's correction. A child before puberty could not have out-thought adult parents in a fair contest; the parents lost because they used their intelligence against itself. ``Dysrationalia'' is Keith Stanovich's term, credited earlier in the book in ``Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People.''}
\cpara{Notes, as a joke, that the correction itself came from experience.}
\cpara{States the moral the young author drew: people who downplay intelligence do not understand it, since self-knowledge, and even learning evolutionary psychology, takes intelligence.}

\cpara{Calls intelligence the unfairest card, and calls the claim that something else matters more a way of turning from that unfairness. The paragraph is in the present tense and does not say whether this is the young author's view or the present one. The postscript revises it in part: ``When I think of poor hands dealt to humans, these days, I think first of death and old age.''}

\cpara{Reports the young author's answer to unfairness: raise everyone's intelligence. The present author corrects the quoted motto (``No one exists only to serve'') but does not regret acting on it. I could not find the motto in the early writings I could reach.}
\cpara{Says the young author claimed no exemption: everyone, the young author included, needed to be smarter, since putting oneself on top is what a villain does.}
\cpara{Lists the obvious traps the young author avoided, and says the present author sees it much the same way.}
\cfact{The archived ``Staring into the Singularity'' (dated 1996 and 1999) bears this out: ``I know, in a dim way, just how dumb I am.''}
\cpara{States the point of the last four paragraphs: the young author did not fail in any obvious way.}
\cpara{Reports meeting the idea of the Singularity in 1996 and deciding at once to work on it; intelligence now seemed even more powerful than before.}
\cstyle{A pun on ``Eureka.'' Eurisko was Douglas Lenat's discovery program, which the author's ``The Plan to Singularity'' (1999--2000) called ``the only attempt at a true artificial mind.''}

\cpara{Applies the Book II term to the author's own case, and gives as the sign of it that the spiral led to false beliefs. The mechanism is the one described in ``Affective Death Spirals''; the notes there discuss the evidence for its feedback step.}

\cfact{I could not find this belief stated in the early texts I could read. ``Staring into the Singularity'' shows the attitude: it likens people who set ``hard limits on Powers'' to fish ``knowing that the entire Universe is wet.''}
\cpara{Names the real wrong turn: the answer given to someone who said that intelligence has nothing to do with being good.}
\cpara{Gives the young author's reasoning: the young author's own ethics had been built with intelligence, and a chimpanzee cannot follow the Prisoner's Dilemma.}

\cpara{The conclusion. The early writings bear out the account. ``Staring into the Singularity'' (archived text dated 1996 and 1999): ``I am reasonably (95\%) certain that the Powers will be ethical''; ``If wiping out your creators is morally wrong, it won't happen.'' ``The Singularitarian Principles'' (2000, revised 2001) looks back: ``There was a point where I was sure that superintelligent meant super-ethical (probably true).'' The parenthesis is the verdict on the claim when that text was written, so it was still held as probable in 2000 or 2001.}

\clogic{The case supplies what the notes on ``Resist the Happy Death Spiral'' found missing there: a false nice claim about a Great Idea that a careful admirer actually made. It also has the form the halo effect describes, one good trait, intelligence, raising the perception of another, goodness.}
\cpara{Ends with an unattributed saying about parents and a promise to continue.}

\cpara{Says what has changed. Death and old age now come first among bad hands; the author no longer works hard to downplay being smart; intelligence is still ``the lever that lifts worlds,'' now seen as part of physics, and whether a superintelligence can travel faster than light depends on the true laws.}
